meta.source: Next Generation Science Standards (NGSS Lead States, 2013), performance expectations
meta.scope_note: Only the performance expectations this program's ocean-robotics material can honestly touch, not all of NGSS: the eight Engineering Design expectations (MS-ETS1-1 to 4 and HS-ETS1-1 to 4) that MATE ROV work and the CS50 float problems practice, plus two Earth and space science expectations (MS-ESS2-6, HS-ESS2-4) about ocean heat and climate that the Argo float background in Profiling Float touches. Not indexed: the Physical Science expectations on forces, energy, waves and circuits, and the Life Science and Earth science expectations about ocean ecosystems, which the ROV lesson cards would need if they are ever aligned; add them then. The three NGSS dimensions behind each expectation (science and engineering practices, disciplinary core ideas, crosscutting concepts) are not indexed separately.
meta.codes_note: Codes are NGSS's own performance expectation codes (grade band, topic, number), used as published. NGSS does not name its expectations; the items here have no `name`, only a paraphrase. Groups are this project's own, by grade band and topic.

items.paraphrase: Spell out what a design problem has to achieve and what limits it (the criteria and constraints) in words precise enough that a solution can be tested against them, thinking about the people affected and the natural world.
Compare several possible solutions to the same problem in a systematic way, judging how well each one meets the criteria and constraints.
Read the data from tests of several solutions to see what each one does well or badly, and use that to pull the best features of each into a better design.
Build and use a model of a proposed object, tool or process, and use the data from testing the model to improve the design again and again.
Take a large real-world challenge and turn it into specific requirements, both qualitative and quantitative, that take the needs of the people involved and the wider effects into account.
Break a complex problem into smaller, more manageable problems that each can be solved with engineering.
Judge a solution against prioritized criteria and the trade-offs among them (cost, safety, reliability, looks), including its social, cultural and environmental effects.
Use a computer simulation to see how a proposed solution behaves across the range of conditions it could face, as a way to test and refine it.

groups.name: Earth and Space Science: Ocean, Heat and Climate

items.paraphrase: Use a model of how the Sun heats the Earth unevenly, and how the Earth spins, to explain the patterns of air and ocean circulation that give different regions their climates.
Use a model to describe how changes in the flow of energy into and out of Earth's systems (the ocean among them) can change the climate.
